name: Helium
utility: Helium (HNT) powers a decentralized wireless network that provides cellular‑grade mobile data and low‑power IoT connectivity by rewarding individuals and businesses who run Hotspot hardware. The network is used by major mobile carriers (e.g., AT&T, Movistar) to offload traffic and by end‑users of Helium Mobile and enterprise venues that need indoor coverage.
evidence: 4,388 TB of carrier‑offloaded data in Q4 2025, a 60.7 % QoQ increase, generating an annualized $11 million revenue run‑rate — Messari “State of Helium Q4 2025” (Mar 5 2026).
2 million+ average daily active users and 120 k+ active Mobile Hotspots in 2025, showing real‑world consumer adoption — Helium “2025 Year in Review” blog (Dec 19 2025).
595,800 Helium Mobile sign‑ups and $75 million in subscriber savings as of Dec 31 2025, indicating a sizable MVNO customer base — Messari report (Q4 2025).
whyNow: In October 2026 Helium announced late‑stage negotiations with AT&T and outlined new venue‑tier reward structures, signaling fresh carrier revenue opportunities and accelerated network deployment.
risks: Reward pauses or accounting errors (e.g., the Cisco Catalyst traffic‑figure correction) can reduce hotspot earnings and deter deployers.
Regulatory uncertainty around the classification of HNT as a security could limit token incentives or impose compliance costs.
profile:
Helium’s business model combines a purpose‑built Layer‑1 blockchain with a “people‑built” wireless infrastructure. Deployers install Hotspots that provide Wi‑Fi or cellular coverage; the network validates coverage (Proof‑of‑Coverage) and data transfer, minting HNT tokens that are burned to purchase Data Credits for traffic. Revenue comes from carrier offload agreements—major carriers pay Helium to route user data through community Hotspots—and from the Helium Mobile MVNO, which bundles HNT‑burned Data Credits into subscription plans. The network’s growth is driven by expanding hotspot density, carrier contracts, and the Helium Plus product that lets existing Wi‑Fi sites join without new hardware.

Competitors include traditional telecom operators building small‑cell/DAS solutions, other DePIN projects (e.g., Althea, DIMO), and satellite‑based broadband providers. A shift in carrier strategy toward in‑house densification, a major regulatory ruling on HNT, or a sustained drop in offload traffic could curtail revenue, while successful large‑venue contracts, broader MVNO adoption, or new enterprise Wi‑Fi Toolkit sales would accelerate utility and token demand.
